item.title: Strait of Hormuz still unsafe for ships, maritime group warns
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
What to know about the Iran war today: Ships remain exposed to "indiscriminate attacks" in the Strait of Hormuz, even if they try to hide their movements by switching off tracking systems, a maritime monitor said Thursday, confirming three strikes on vessels in the waterway this week.The Saudi-led coalition battling the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen said Thursday it had intercepted a cruise missile over Saudi Arabia's western Medina region. The Houthis called the claim " a shameless and brazen lie ."President Trump has said he's considering joining the Saudi-led attacks on the Houthis as the rebels threaten global energy supplies. The Houthis have threatened to target U.S. personnel and interests across the Middle East if Mr. Trump does order strikes, which could drag the U.S. deeper into the wider 7-and-a-half-month war . Trump administration considering easing Iran sanctions to reduce shipping costs, Reuters says The United States is considering easing sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet tankers to reduce record-high global shipping costs, the Reuters news agency reported Thursday, citing an unnamed U.S. official. The proposal would allow companies, subject to U.S. Treasury approval, to transport non-sanctioned oil on previously sanctioned vessels, according to the Reuters report. However, the move would be unlikely to significantly lower freight rates, as many tankers are old and insurers would remain bound by EU and U.K. restrictions, market analysis firm Energy Aspects told its clients, Reuters reported. The discussions are reportedly taking place days after President Trump paused sanctions on Russian diesel , a decision criticized by Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, European nations and some Republicans in the U.S. Senate. U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright told the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh via video that the measure would not facilitate Russian oil shipments, Energy Aspects told clients. 2 men convicted in Germany of planning attacks on pro-Israel figures on behalf of Iran A German court on Thursday jailed two men convicted of planning attacks on prominent pro-Israel public figures and spying on Jews on behalf of Iranian secret services. The court in Hamburg sentenced a Danish national named as Ali S. to eight-and-a-half years in prison for planning deadly attacks on targets including the head of the German-Israeli society, Volker Beck, and the head of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster. An Afghan accomplice, Tawab M., was sentenced to four-and-a-half years in prison. Prosecutors said he had agreed to recruit a third man and provide him with a weapon for the attack on Beck. S. took orders from the Quds Force, the elite foreign operations branch of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, in early 2025, prosecutors said. The two men were remanded in custody in Germany following their arrests and extraditions last year in Denmark. Their convictions came days after Britain's domestic spy chief warned of Iran's evolving "hybrid tactics" aimed largely at Jewish communities and groups in the U.K. and across Europe. CBS/AFP EU and Persian Gulf nations postpone summit in Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks A summit between the European Union and Persian Gulf countries that was scheduled to take place at the end of this month in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh has been postponed, the EU said Thursday, as Saudi Arabia faces attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels. "The second Summit between the European Union and the Gulf Cooperation Council, originally planned for 24 October 2026 in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, has been postponed. A new date will be announced in due course," the EU's governing body, the European Council, said in a statement. The Saudi-led coalition fighting in support of Yemen's government said Thursday it had intercepted a ballistic missile in the region of Medina. The Houthis swiftly denied launching an attack on the Islamic kingdom's second holiest city. CBS/AFP Yemen urges U.N. to take urgent action to lift Houthi siege of Taiz Yemen's government has urged the United Nations and the U.N. Security Council to take urgent action to end what it described as a tightening Houthi siege of the southwest city of Taiz, warning of a looming humanitarian catastrophe affecting more than four million people. In a letter sent on Wednesday to senior U.N. officials and the International Committee of the Red Cross, Foreign Minister Afrah Al-Zouba warned that the Houthis' escalating siege on the government-held city had worsened humanitarian conditions, including in areas around Taiz where displaced people have sought shelter. The government called in its statement for the immediate lifting of the Houthi siege, the reopening of all access routes for civilians and supply chains, and unimpeded access to food, fuel and water. It also urged stronger monitoring and accountability mechanisms to document alleged violations and hold those responsible to account. Al-Zouba called for concrete international measures to protect civilians and prevent access to humanitarian essentials being used for political pressure. She said the situation required urgent action beyond expressions of concern, including ending the siege, restoring essential supplies and protecting civilian facilities. Saudi Arabia says cruise missile intercepted in the kingdom's Medina region The Saudi-led coalition battling the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen said Thursday that it had intercepted a cruise missile over the Medina region in western Saudi Arabia. "Interception and destruction of a cruise missile in the Medina region," coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said in a post on X . He did not say where the missile came from, but the Houthis, who have been peppering the kingdom with airstrikes over the past week, said "the Saudi enemy's claims of an attack on Medina are a shameless and brazen lie ." Medina is the second holiest city in Islam, after Mecca. In September, the Saudis accused the Houthis of attacking Mecca, the holiest city for Muslims, which they denied. "Strait of Hormuz is closed," says Iranian naval officer, citing U.S. gas prices An Iranian naval officer renewed Iran's claim on Thursday that the Strait of Hormuz is closed, saying U.S. gas prices wouldn't be so high otherwise. "The Strait of Hormuz is closed; if it were not closed, oil would be passing through it and gas prices in the United States would not have increased," Iranian Army Coordination Deputy Rear Admiral Habibollah Sayyari told reporters on the sidelines of a ceremony honouring army nurses in Tehran, according to Iran's official IRNA news agency . He said the naval forces of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' had a strong presence west of the strait, while the Iranian army was deployed east of the waterway and as far north as the Gulf of Oman, exercising what he called "100% control and supervision" over the area. "If any transit takes place, it must be coordinated; otherwise, you can see in the news what happens," Sayyari said. Ships in Strait of Hormuz remain exposed to "indiscriminate attacks," says monitor, as 3 more strikes confirmed Ships in the Strait of Hormuz remain exposed to "indiscriminate attacks," regardless of the nations to which they are registered, the cargo they are carrying, their direction of travel, or whether they turn off their tracking devices, Greek maritime monitor Marisks said Thursday. Marisks said it had confirmed that three merchant vessels were struck by unidentified projectiles on Tuesday - incidents it said "demonstrate the indiscriminate nature of the current threat environment in the Strait of Hormuz." Marisks said the vessels were all navigating with their tracking devices turned off, a common tactic for boats trying to get through the waterway unnoticed, which shows it "does not provide effective protection against attack," the monitor said. The continued strikes on vessels in the strait show that, "although successful passages continue," ships in the strait are exposing themselves to a "critical and highly unpredictable maritime security threat," Marisks wrote, "with merchant vessels exposed to potentially indiscriminate attacks regardless of flag, cargo or direction of transit." Three of the ships struck this week were operated by the same firm, they added in their bulletin, which also "raises concerns regarding possible operator-linked targeting." Tehran must be prepared for war amid peace talks, Iran's parliament speaker says Iran must be prepared for war even as it negotiates with the U.S., the country's parliament speaker said Wednesday. Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf said in a televised speech that his country's main concern is preventing the U.S. from attacking again. But, he added, a signed agreement with Washington is no guarantee. "They break their promises," said Qalibaf. As a result, Iran must be prepared to fight "against a bullying enemy," and "we must truly fight courageously on the battlefield." "That is when we will have achieved sustainable deterrence," he said. "America must be punished. America must change its behavior. It must understand that it has to come to terms with the Iranian people." Trump on reports U.S. considering Iran strikes before midterms: "Leakers should be shot" Speaking about news reports that the U.S. is considering potential strikes against Iran before the midterms in November, President Trump said Wednesday it was his opinion that "leakers should be shot." "In the old days, we used to shoot leakers," Mr. Trump said during a campaign rally speech in Bullhead City, Arizona. "When they leak what time you're going to attack a country, and the reason you're attacking is really for defense, because you don't want them to have a weapon that can blow up millions of people in one shot." "Now, leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly," he added. "To me, they're the scum of the earth." The Atlantic first reported on Oct. 7 that the Pentagon was developing strike options against Iranian targets, but no final decisions had been made. The next day, the president said on Truth Social that the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections, which take place on Nov. 3. U.S. military destroyed Iran-affiliated vessel in Gulf of Oman last week, CENTCOM says U.S. forces destroyed an Iran-affiliated vessel in the Gulf of Oman last week, the U.S. Central Command said on Wednesday. CENTCOM said the dhow, a generic name for an Arab sailing vessel, was conducting surveillance and targeting U.S. Navy ships. The ship's crew members were "safely removed prior to destruction of the dhow," the military command said in a social media post . It's unclear if the crew members were taken into custody or released. Yemen wants training, intelligence assistance from U.S., foreign minister says Yemen has asked the U.S. for training and intelligence support for the Yemeni armed forces and coast guard, as well as continued political, economic and humanitarian support, but their foreign minister made no mention of military support in a briefing to reporters Wednesday. Afrah Alzouba, Yemen's first female foreign minister, spoke in a briefing on several topics related to the ongoing Yemen-Houthi war, but did not explicitly mention requests for military support. In addition to intelligence and training, Alzouba requested the U.S. expand sanctions against the Houthis. She also asked for the EU and Washington to coordinate more closely on sanctions. She struck an aggressive tone when asked about possible negotiations with the Houthi militia, saying, "We are not calling for starting any negotiations." The Yemeni government eventually wants a peaceful settlement but is prioritizing military operations to end Houthi control, she said. She also emphasized Yemeni ownership of ongoing operations with air support from coalition partners: "The decision is Yemeni. The command is Yemeni. The soldiers are Yemenis." The Saudis are the strongest backers of the official Yemeni government forces, which has earned the ire of the Houthis. They have repeatedly targeted civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, including a strike that killed 13 people at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport. A four-year ceasefire between the two sides fell apart this summer. Alzouba said the contacts cited last month by President Trump between the U.S. and Houthis, which surprised some in the U.S., involved "warnings" against further attacks. She did not elaborate on timing or channels. A look at the Iran- and Russia-linked hybrid attacks the U.K. spy chief says are flourishing The head of Britain's top domestic spy agency MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, painted a dark picture Tuesday of the changing national security threats facing the U.K. and the world. "We have entered a new era of national security, requiring a new response," he said in his annual threat update at MI5 headquarters in London. "Those who mean the U.K. harm aren't attacking things government owns or controls. … They're aiming at people, businesses, communities." Iran has used and continues "using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations, and Israeli sites," McCallum said. But analysts have also seen "Iran, like Russia, attempting to expand their hybrid campaign," he said, leading to more than 50 arrests in the U.K. over the last year alone. "Sadly, much of this aggression has been aimed at British Jewish communities," McCallum said, speaking of incidents this year that included "a wave of arson and sabotage incidents targeting Jewish communities in the U.K. and other European nations," but also acts targeting "harder targets, like military sites." Read more here . Attacks in Strait of Hormuz reach highest level since start of war, data shows At least 10 vessels have been attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz since Sunday, a high since war broke out between the United States, Israel and Iran, security data showed Wednesday. Four vessels were struck on Tuesday and six on Sunday — the highest number of attacks in a single day since the start of the conflict — according to data from security firm Vanguard, the International Maritime Organization and the British maritime agency UKMTO. Two seafarers have been reported missing and a container ship reportedly sank as a result of recent attacks, according to the maritime sources. Merchant vessels transiting the vital passage were first targeted by Iran in March in retaliation for U.S.-Israeli strikes on its territory, and Tehran has continued to strike vessels passing through the strait via routes it has not approved. The attacks have disrupted shipping through the strait, which is normally one of the busiest routes for exporting oil and other commodities from Gulf countries. Twenty-three attacks have been recorded since the start of October, almost double the average monthly number of incidents since the start of the war. "Gulf oil flows have been recovering, with traffic through Hormuz recently returning to around 80 percent of pre-war levels despite the conflict," Vanguard analyst Barun Gupta told AFP on Wednesday. "Increasing the tempo of attacks therefore gives Tehran a way of demonstrating that it can still disrupt that recovery and impose costs on commercial shipping and global energy markets," Gupta continued. Yemeni government speaks to Chinese officials about Houthis developing advanced missiles The Yemeni government has spoken with Beijing about the Houthis' alleged attempts to utilize Chinese-made technology for weapons, a Yemeni minister said on Wednesday. "The Chinese are partners and we have discussed with them about, you know, the use of dual products," Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba said in response to an AFP question about reports the Iran-backed group was trying to secure Chinese components to help manufacture weapons. "They were very keen for any sort of information so they can investigate it. Their support to the Yemeni government is clear," Zouba added. The minister spoke to journalists via a virtual press conference to address the war in Yemen, which has also drawn in the government's main backer, Saudi Arabia. The comments came after a recent report by the Conflict Armament Research group alleged the Houthis were attempting to produce advanced medium-range ballistic missiles. Conflict Armament Research also suggested the group was "expanding its supply chains beyond Iran-linked supply networks, with several purpose-built missile components found alongside shipping documents that listed a Chinese supplier." Saudi-Houthi war in Yemen cutting off food assistance to 800,000 people, U.N. says The escalating war between the Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces is cutting off lifesaving food supplies to about 800,000 people in the region, according to the U.N. World Food Programme . Many parts of Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, which is located in Houthi-controlled territory, is completely inaccessible to the nonprofit, the WFP said. There are more than 600,000 people, including 200,000 women and children, in Taiz who depend on humanitarian aid, according to the agency. "We are critically concerned about the escalating conflict, but even more so about the growing number of people we can no longer reach because of it," El-Khidir Daloum, WFP representative and country director in Yemen, said in a statement Wednesday. "Many of the families affected have been displaced multiple times and were already struggling to afford even basic food items. This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe if assistance cannot move safely and reach those who need it most." The hunger situation in Yemen is among the worst in the world. Ten out of 16 districts in Yemen are categorized as being at emergency levels of food insecurity, the WFP said. About 500,000 children in Yemen under the age of 5 suffer from severe acute malnutrition, according to the group. There are also 37 WFP employees currently being held by the Houthis, the group said, calling for their immediate release. Saudi Arabia postpones Netflix tennis tournament featuring top stars The chairman of Saudi Arabia's General Entertainment Authority on Wednesday said the exhibition Six Kings Slam tennis tournament has been postponed for logistical reasons, after Yemen's Houthis carried out several deadly attacks on the kingdom. "The Six Kings Slam tournament has been postponed due to logistical reasons and will now take place on December 27," wrote Turki Alalshikh on X, sharing a statement from the Riyadh Season entertainment program. The tournament, while not officially sanctioned as an ATP event, features some of the top players in the world vying for millions of dollars and airs live on Netflix. It had initially been scheduled to air Oct. 21 to 24. The men's-only event features Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic, Alexander Zverev, Taylor Fritz, Alex De Minaur and Learner Tien, who replaced Jannik Sinner due to injury. The event premiered in 2024 with Sinner winning each of the first two competitions. Sinner, Alcaraz, Djokovic or Zverev has won every major since Wimbledon in 2022. CBS/AFP Israel signs deal with Pentagon to acquire 12 Apache attack helicopters Israel has signed a deal with the Pentagon to acquire 12 Apache helicopters from Boeing, according to the Israeli Ministry of Defense. "The procurement of Apache helicopters is a critical step in building the IDF's force capabilities; it will strengthen operational readiness against a wide range of threats and contribute to the security of the State of Israel for years to come," Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said in a statement. The helicopters, the newest Apache E model, can carry 16 HELLFIRE missiles, 76 2.75-inch rockets and 1,200 30 mm chain gun rounds, according to Boeing. While the deal was signed Wednesday, it will be a while before they are in combat. They are "scheduled for delivery early next decade," according to the Israeli defense ministry. Israel already has older models of the Apache helicopter. Israel agreed to buy a second squadron of F-15IA fighter jets from Boeing earlier this year. They initially purchased a squadron in 2024. Hassett blames disappointing inflation numbers on Houthi attacks Kevin Hassett, the White House's top economic adviser, blamed the disappointing inflation numbers for September on attacks against Saudi oil assets. "What happened was that because the Houthis started attacking the Saudi pipeline and other Iranian proxies from Iraq were attacking refineries and so on, we had a negative shock to energy again in September," Hassett told Fox Business on Wednesday. "A lot of Trump policies are helping to keep inflation down, but the energy shock is really the headline story today," he said. Hassett said much of the energy concerns had "abated," and while the East-West pipeline is back up and running, the Houthis have also stepped up attacks in Saudi Arabia. In addition to targeting civilian airports, they have targeted Aramco, the world's largest oil producer, facilities and even the executive headquarters overnight Wednesday. The price of Brent crude, the international standard for oil, was hovering around $105 on Wednesday, up from $98 on the last day of September. Saudi offers alternative travel routes for investment conference: AFP sources Saudi Arabia plans to move ahead with a major investment conference in Riyadh despite Houthi attacks on the kingdom, offering on-site and virtual attendance as well as alternative air and land travel routes, diplomatic sources told AFP. Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events, but it has recently seen escalating military tensions with the Iran-backed Yemeni group, which has intensified attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil facilities. Saudi Arabia's Future Investment Initiative Institute hosts an annual forum dubbed "Davos in the desert," which usually draws foreign leaders and business titans, and this year it is scheduled to be held in Riyadh from Oct. 26 to 29. In order to prevent cancellation, organizers reached out to embassies and foreign companies to explore "hybrid" participation options, allowing officials and business executives to attend either in person or virtually, diplomatic sources said. They have even discussed arrangements for participants to fly by private jet to Dhahran airport in eastern Saudi Arabia before traveling by road to Riyadh. A diplomat from an Asian country said "they contacted us and offered that attendees travel to Manama or Doha," referring to the capitals of Bahrain and Qatar respectively, and then drive by land to the Saudi capital. Riyadh's international airport, a main target for Houthi attacks, suspended operations last week after 13 were killed in a strike there, with no clear timeline for when air traffic would reopen. U.S. inflation accelerated to 3.7% as energy costs soared Inflation accelerated across the U.S. in September, rising at an annual rate of 3.7% as energy prices soared, according to new government data. Inflation picked up after two months of holding steady at an annual pace of 3.4%. Core CPI, which excludes the more volatile energy and gas categories, rose 2.6% from a year ago, accelerating from a 2.4% rate in August and higher than economists' forecast of 2.5%. Inflation has risen sharply since the start of the year due to soaring energy prices, sparked by the war in Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine. The Labor Department said Wednesday that gasoline prices, which rose 9.1% in September from the prior month, accounted for more than half the monthly increase in the CPI report. Energy prices rose 20.4% from a year ago, while gasoline jumped 34.2%. Prices at the pump have cooled slightly in recent weeks but remain elevated. The national average for a gallon of gasoline was $4.33 a gallon on Wednesday, AAA reported, up from $2.98 before the war started. The national average for diesel, which hit a record high in late September, was $6.29 a gallon. Read more here . Lebanese, Iranian foreign leaders discuss situation in the Middle East Lebanese President Joseph Aoun received a call from Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Wednesday to discuss the situation in the Middle East, according to the Lebanese president's office. Both sides "discussed the current situation in the region in light of recent developments and agreed on the necessity of supporting diplomatic solutions as the best means to put an end to the conflicts in the region," the Lebanese presidency said in a statement about the call. The Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group has been waging war with Israel in the southern part of Lebanon for months, with the official Lebanese government attempting to cool the conflict down with ceasefire agreements. Those have all been dismissed and ignored by Hezbollah. Meanwhile, Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh arrived in Lebanon for talks with several groups. He was greeted by Lebanese Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, who is pro-Hezbollah, and other Hezbollah representatives, according to the official Iranian news outlet IRNA. The meeting comes amid an increase in attacks by another Iran-backed proxy group, the Yemen-based Houthis. "During his visit, Khatibzadeh is scheduled to hold a series of meetings with senior Lebanese officials and prominent figures to discuss bilateral relations and explore opportunities to broaden cooperation between the two countries," according to IRNA. 2 more ships attacked in Hormuz: U.K. navy reports Two ships sustained minor damage after coming under attack in the Strait of Hormuz, a British maritime agency reported Wednesday. Both vessels were struck on Tuesday by an "unknown projectile," bringing to four the number of attacks on ships in Hormuz that day. Iran and the United States continue to vie for control of the waterway, a vital shipping route for Gulf energy exports. Tehran regularly targets ships it accuses of transiting without its permission, while Washington has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre said a 50,000-ton container ship and another 19,000-ton vessel were struck but continued on their way after sustaining only minor damage. No casualties were reported in the attacks. British security firm Vanguard also said attacks had targeted four ships. It identified the vessels as the GFS Pride and GFS Giselle, both sailing under Singaporean flags, and the Alfonso, which was flying a Barbados flag. The fourth ship was identified as the Al Saadiyat, sailing under the Marshall Islands flag. According to Vanguard, the GFS Pride, a container ship, sank , while the fate of the Alfonso, a tanker, remains unknown. Iran says cargo ship sinks after hitting naval mine in Strait of Hormuz Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Wednesday that a cargo ship had sunk after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz. It is the first time Iran has reported a ship sinking after hitting a mine during the war. There were few details, including about the fate of the crew. Iranian state TV quoted a statement from the IRGC saying the ship was traveling on what Iran considers an illegal and dangerous route - likely the shipping lanes the U.S. has urged vessels to use, close to Oman's coast - when it hit the mine Wednesday morning. It said the ship was carrying 2,500 containers when it first caught fire. Iran has repeatedly warned ships against trying to transit the strait without its approval. At the end of August, President Trump declared the strait free of sea mines , saying U.S. forces had "totally cleared the strait of mines … Any boat goes through with a mine, we take it out." There was no immediate verification of the sinking and no report by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations monitor. CBS/AP Houthis warn attacks on Saudi airports, oil infrastructure will continue The Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said Wednesday that they would continue targeting Saudi Arabia's international airport and oil infrastructure in the coming days. In a televised statement, Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the attacks were "in response to the treacherous Saudi aggression against the capital Sanaa and the free governorates" and part of the group's "deterrence operations against the Saudi aggressor." Saree also warned international shipping companies, civilians, and employees working at the targeted airports and businesses to "stay away from them and evacuate them immediately," as they would be considered legitimate targets. Saudis say another Houthi ballistic missile targeting Riyadh was intercepted A spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition forces said Wednesday they had intercepted an attack from the Iran-backed Houthi militia. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said in a post on X a ballistic missile "launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh has been intercepted and destroyed." Earlier, residents in the Saudi capital had reported hearing explosions. Residents in Saudi Arabia's capital say they have heard new explosions in Riyadh Residents in Saudi Arabia's capital say they have heard new explosions in Riyadh. The residents spoke on condition of anonymity for their safety. One lives in northern Riyadh, where King Khalid International Airport is located. The source of the explosions wasn't immediately clear. The Saudi civil defense reported air raid alerts in Riyadh and Kharj province southeast of the capital. Kharj is home to the state-owned Military Industries Corporation and Prince Sultan Air Base. The airport in Riyadh has been targeted several times in the past week with deadly attacks. Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen have claimed responsibility. Intercepted missiles over Riyadh injure at least 4 people, officials say Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense said debris from two intercepted Houthi missiles fell on residential areas in Riyadh on Tuesday, injuring four people and damaging 15 homes. State-run Saudi Press Agency reported the injured included two women, a man and a child. Images released by Saudi's Civil Defense showed broken windows caused by what it said was fallen shrapnel. CBS/AP Building fire reported in Aramco compound targeted by Houthis, Saudi officials say The Saudi Ministry of Energy said Tuesday a limited fire broke out in an administrative building in Aramco, one of the world's largest oil facilities, that was targeted in the country's Eastern Province. The ministry said no injuries were reported. The attack comes as the Iranian-backed Houthis and the Saudi coalition exchanged attacks Tuesday night. It marks a fresh escalation in the widening Middle East crisis and came shortly after the Saudi coalition reported a series of alerts for incoming missiles heading for the country's Eastern Province, a major oil-producing region and the capital Riyadh. Saudi-led forces confirm strikes on Yemen oil sites The Saudi-led coalition battling the Iran-backed Houthis confirmed it struck oil sites across western Yemen on Tuesday, including in the capital Sanaa, in response to the deadliest attack on the kingdom's soil in years. Blasts were heard shortly after in Saudi capital Riyadh and at an oil giant Aramco facility in eastern Saudi Arabia, witnesses and journalists told AFP. Tuesday's coalition strikes in Yemen's Sanaa and the western provinces of Dhamar and Saada targeted facilities used to "supply the war effort" by the Houthis to "threaten the kingdom, Yemen, the southern Red Sea and waterways," coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki wrote on X. An AFP correspondent in Sanaa reported an explosion, while a breaking news alert on the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV channel said earlier that "Saudi aggression" targeted the oil firm. item.title: Putrajaya Paying RM130,000 Each To Four FDS Crash Victims’ Families
item.description:
Source: CodeBlue (Malaysia Health)

item.title: Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian refineries as Zelensky says 'we're done' with truce
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Daniel Flynn and Max Hunder KYIV, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery on Thursday, after President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Kyiv was "done" supporting a ceasefire on energy targets announced by US President Donald Trump and ignored by Russia. Since Trump's surprise announcement on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on energy, Kyiv had suspended attacks on Russian refineries, which Trump blames for raising diesel ‌prices on global markets. But in the days that followed, Russia rained down deadly missile and drone strikes, including on energy targets such as power stations, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of people. In an interview ‌with the Financial Times published on Thursday, Zelenskiy said Ukraine's patience had run out. "The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We're done," he told the newspaper. Zelenskiy also made clear he believed that changes in the capability of the military version of SpaceX's Starlink receptors this week, which have curbed Ukraine's ability to ​use them to pilot its drones, were a policy decision. "It was not a technical problem, it was the will," he told the FT. In a social media post overnight, SpaceX boss Elon Musk said usage of the military version of Starlink, known as Starshield, was ultimately up to Trump, as president of the United States. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk wrote. BIGGEST RIFT WITH WASHINGTON OF THE WAR By effectively walking away from Trump's demand that Ukraine halt attacks on refineries, Zelenskiy risks deepening the biggest rift between Kyiv and Washington since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Although Trump has described the ceasefire as a requirement for both Moscow and Kyiv, his public comments have ‌focused mainly on Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries, which he said over the weekend ⁠had "damn well better stop". Trump has long had a testy relationship with Zelenskiy and berated him in the White House in February 2025. But his sharp turn against Kyiv in recent days has little precedent. He first angered Ukraine last week by abruptly lifting sanctions on Russian diesel, and then called on Ukraine to replace Zelenskiy. Ukrainians worry that the rift could have severe consequences on the ⁠battlefield, where the Ukrainian military still depends on technology provided by Washington. Over the past several days, Ukrainian officials have reported that they have not received the usual warnings from Western allies about incoming Russian missiles, which rely on US satellite detectors. Trump has denied withholding intelligence. Zelenskiy said the failure to provide the warnings had been presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch. At the same time, military-grade Starlink receptors have stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance ​systems ​over Ukrainian territory. A source in Ukraine's defence ministry said on Thursday that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds ​of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kph). Ukrainian officials have said that is too ‌slow for mid-range attack missions and interceptor drones that defend against Russian drones. REFINERY SUPPLYING MOSCOW HIT Ukraine has been using its long-range drones to target Russian refineries and logistics in recent months, which it says is its only answer to nearly five years of relentless Russian bombardment. The attacks have caused fuel shortages in Russia. Trump, under pressure to lower fuel prices, especially for diesel which has reached record highs since he launched a war against Iran in February, says the Ukrainian attacks are driving up global prices. Ukraine's latest target was a refinery in the Ryazan region southeast of Moscow, which is owned by state oil major Rosneft and accounts for nearly 5% of Russia's refinery throughput, helping supply the capital. Regional governor Pavel Malkov said in a post on Telegram that a major Ukrainian drone attack had caused a fire at the refinery. Damage was being assessed and emergency services were at the scene. A Ukrainian official confirmed that Ukraine had hit a Russian refinery overnight in response to Moscow's heavy ballistic ‌missile and drone attacks this week that violated the energy truce. In the latest attacks on Ukraine, three people were killed and six wounded ​in the central region of Kirovohrad overnight, as Russia launched more than 500 drones. State-owned energy company Naftogaz said a gas extraction facility in ​Poltava was damaged and operations were suspended. The Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure ran ​counter to US peace efforts. It said earlier this week that the scope of the energy ceasefire had never been determined and work was still ongoing to do so. BREAKDOWN IN RELATIONS In the FT ‌interview, Zelenskiy criticised Washington’s eagerness to strike business deals with Moscow and Trump’s apparent admiration ​for Russia's Vladimir Putin. The rift has raised concern in Kyiv and ​European capitals about the heavy reliance in Ukraine on US intelligence and technology. Under Trump, Washington has already halted weapons supplies to Ukraine while allowing its European allies to continue buying US arms on Kyiv's behalf. But Europe has no ready-made alternatives to Starlink, or to US satellite systems used to detect Russian missile launches. Zelenskiy has said that Ukrainian military officials had been warned by US counterparts that Washington would block intelligence unless they halted strikes on ​Russian energy infrastructure. Asked whether Ukraine would be open to halting energy strikes as a way ‌of repairing relations with the White House, Zelenskiy told the newspaper he could agree only if in return he were given more US-made Patriot interceptors, calling it the “minimum” that would be acceptable. Ukraine's navy said on ​Thursday it had destroyed six Russian Su-34M military aircraft in an overnight strike on the Borisoglebsk airfield in Russia's Voronezh region. The navy said on Telegram it used its Neptune coastal missile system in ​the attack. (Reporting by Daniel Flynn, Max Hunder, Dan Peleschuk, and Lina GolovnyaEditing by Tom Hogue, Edwina Gibbs, Jason Neely, Peter Graff) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/zelenskiy-says-ukraine-resume-strikes-060307306.html

item.title: Six Flags faced warnings about ride safety long before this week's roller coaster death
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A man died after being ejected from the Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags in Austell, Georgia, on Monday. - Emilie Megnien/AP In the years leading up to this week’s fatal accident at its Georgia theme park, Six Flags has been accused of failing to maintain its parks amid hundreds of reports of injuries and dangerous malfunctions on its aging thrill rides, according to a CNN analysis of public records and court filings. Six Flags temporarily closed 10 rides in seven states this week after 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem fell to his death and several others were injured while riding the Goliath rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia just outside Atlanta. In the last five years, safety records covering more than a dozen parks across three different states reveal maintenance issues, such as a train derailment, faulty restraint bars and guest injuries including dislocated joints and concussions. Six Flags is the country’s largest theme park operator – with 30 water and amusement parks in 13 states. In a statement to CNN, the company said it was “committed to rigorous ride inspection, maintenance and safety procedures that meet or exceed industry standards.” But Six Flags has struggled financially amid weak attendance and crushing debt following a 2024 merger with competitor Cedar Fair, according to its financial statements from recent years. Two investor lawsuits filed last year allege that prior to the merger, Six Flags officials had put off basic park maintenance, infrastructure repairs and ride updates as it slashed employee headcount. In investor calls last year cited in the lawsuits, a Six Flags executive described a need to invest in “deferred items” at the amusement parks, while another stated the “list is always long” for needed improvements in response to a question from a financial analyst. Six Flags has not responded to the lawsuits’ claims in court. Kariem was a “cherished" teacher and robotics coach at Wesley International Academy, a public charter school in Atlanta. - Wesley International Academy The company “failed to make adequate capital investments to conduct routine facility maintenance or improve rides and attractions, and made drastic personnel cuts,” according to one investor lawsuit. The other alleges Six Flags “had for years deferred or foregone” necessary repairs. The safety of Six Flags rides had already come under fire this summer, after a CNN investigation exposed how one of its most famous roller coasters, X2 at Six Flags Magic Mountain, had been linked to more than a dozen serious brain injuries, hospitalizations and even deaths. Officials had kept the ride open for nearly two decades despite a long history of problems. But last month, the company closed it permanently after CNN reported that two women had been rushed into emergency brain surgery six days apart in July and more than 100 injured riders came forward with brain injury claims. This week’s fatal accident in Georgia comes less than two weeks after the high-profile closure of X2, which officials attributed to a loss of guest confidence in the ride. The president of Six Flags over Georgia said in a statement that the park has “a comprehensive safety program built on rigorous inspections” for each ride and is cooperating with state investigators while also conducting its own review of the incident. This aerial view shows the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, California, on Sept. 23, 2026. - Jae C. Hong/AP Six Flags did not comment on the injuries reported to various state regulators but said all reported guest injuries are “taken seriously” and reviewed. Officials also said that the incidents reviewed by CNN “span multiple parks, attractions, years, jurisdictions and circumstances, and may reflect differing state reporting requirements and a wide range of incidents and outcomes. As a result, broad conclusions drawn from a compilation of reports may not provide the full context surrounding any individual event or our overall approach to safety.” unknown content item - Theme park-related accidents remain rare, with an industry report showing roughly 1,500 injuries in 2024. Most of these were classified as related to guest behavior or medical conditions, and roughly 25 percent were caused by technical or operational issues, such as mechanical problems with a ride or operator error. “There is always the possibility of mechanical failure in spite of following all the standards and other specific procedures developed by manufacturers and operators,” Edward Pribonic, an amusement ride engineer and ride safety expert who has served as an expert witness on behalf of plaintiffs suing Six Flags, said in an email. “However, recurring safety incidents and mechanical failures usually point to a lack of attention to standards and manufacturer’s requirements for whatever reasons.” Typically, these reasons are budget contraints or “incompetence,” he said. In California, state law requires operators to report accidents “where maintenance, operation, or use of the permanent amusement ride results in a death or serious injury to any person unless the injury does not require medical service other than ordinary first aid.” Since 2021, regulators in the state have fielded nearly 300 accident reports from Six Flags parks. The details about each incident were limited and some could involve other factors such as heat or underlying medical conditions. Issues documented included chemical burns and hydraulic fluid that leaked from a ride into someone’s eye, dislocated joints, concussions and broken bones. Across the country at Six Flags Great Adventure in New Jersey, state records showed similar injuries and malfunctions. For instance, park officials reported a 2024 train derailment due to an equipment failure that caused minor injuries and repeated instances of lap bars opening mid-ride – sometimes due to broken bolts. Riders had to evacuate its log ride on seven separate occasions because of issues such as boats colliding or becoming jammed and smoke coming from a malfunctioning part of the ride. And a child was transported for medical treatment after hitting his head multiple times on a roller coaster’s restraint bar. A wooden roller coaster, which is called El Toro and goes up to 70 miles per hour with a steep 176-foot drop, has been the subject of repeated safety reports and ongoing lawsuits in the past five years. In August of 2022, for example, more than a dozen people were injured after experiencing a violent jolt during the ride, according to court filings and state records reviewed by CNN. A month later, the state deemed the ride “structurally compromised” and the ride remained closed until June 2023, according to the legal complaint. In Texas, many injury reports made to state regulators involved water park attractions, such as incidents in which riders were thrown from inner tubes, resulting in head injuries and other trauma. Other reports detail an 8-year-old breaking his arm after his legs got caught in the seat of a children’s ride, a 21-year-old who couldn’t move after riding on a roller coaster because of a back injury and a 37-year-old man who felt his neck “pop” after riding a different attraction and reported his hands going numb and almost fainting. Riders were evacuated from the Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags in Georgia on Monday. - WXIA One guest at Six Flags Over Texas died more than a decade ago under circumstance s similar to this week’s tragedy in Georgia. In that case, which also received national attention, Rosa Esparza, 52, died after being ejected from the Texas Giant roller coaster. Witnesses reported hearing a popping sound before Esparza went flying, and employees told police investigators that maintenance had fixed faulty sensors on the ride a few days prior. Police also heard from a man who claimed he had been injured on the same ride eight years earlier “when the safety bar didn’t properly hold me down” and a woman whose daughter had recorded the ride malfunctioning a week before Esparza’s death, with video showing the restraint bar spontaneously opening up before the ride left the station, records show. In a statement at the time, Six Flags said an investigation had revealed that there had been no mechanical failure on the ride. The roller coaster r eopened two months after Esparza’s death with a number of new safety measures, including a newly designed T-bar restraint and seat belts. CNN has requested data from other states where Six Flags operates, including Georgia, but officials have not yet responded. Do you have information to share about a Six Flags theme park or ride? item.title: Supreme Court sides with GOP in fight over discounted ads ahead of midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By John Kruzel WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court again sided with Republicans on Wednesday in the latest clash over a new Federal Communications Commission policy that gives party committees access to discounted TV and radio advertising rates long available to political candidates. The court agreed to ‌let the FCC, which is chaired by Trump ally Brendan Carr, avoid a judicially imposed deadline that would have forced the agency to rule ‌on a Democratic challenge to the policy before the November 3 midterm elections. The FCC joined two Republican committees in filing a request to the Supreme Court to lift the lower court's deadline. The court ​has a 6-3 conservative majority. Liberal Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated they would have denied the request. The FCC, which currently has a 2-1 Republican majority, modified its so-called "lowest unit charge" rule in March in a move seen as a boost to President Donald Trump's fellow Republicans. The president's party is seeking to retain control of Congress in the November 3 midterms. "We are pleased the Supreme Court has granted the FCC's stay request. The court's decision is right on the law and avoids the specter of upending ‌the rules for political ads right in the middle of ⁠an ongoing election," an FCC spokesperson said. Chief Justice John Roberts had previously lifted the October 9 deadline that was given to the FCC by the Richmond-based 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals. The 4th Circuit has accused the FCC of repeated "delay tactics" in ⁠the case, and emphasized the need for an urgent ruling in the Democratic challenge given the looming election. The Supreme Court's latest action marks the second time in recent weeks that it has addressed the FCC's policy, as major Republican committees head toward the midterms with a cash advantage over their Democratic counterparts. In September, the court granted a request by the national Republican ​committees ​that support the party's candidates in Senate and House of Representatives races to revive the policy ​after the 4th Circuit blocked it. The justices in an ‌8-1 ruling said that the Democratic candidates must wait for the FCC to rule before filing a challenge in court. The FCC policy at issue requires broadcasters to charge discounted rates for airing certain political advertisements within 60 days of a general election, a window that opened this year on September 4. A group of Democratic candidates including Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia in April challenged the policy through in-house proceedings at the FCC. When the agency took no action, the Democrats successfully challenged the policy in the 4th Circuit, a ruling that was later halted by the Supreme Court. The 4th Circuit on October 7 ordered the FCC to issue a prompt ruling on the ‌Democratic in-house challenge, more than five months after it was filed. In its 2-1 ruling, the ​4th Circuit said its "willingness to tolerate the FCC's delay tactics is at an end." 'TRENCH WARFARE' The Republican committees ​in their Supreme Court filing accused the 4th Circuit of having "short-circuited" the ​FCC's review process. The Democratic candidates, for their part, accused the FCC in court papers of engaging in "blatant procedural trench warfare to stave ‌off judicial review of an unlawful agency directive until it is ​too late to matter." The FCC policy gained ​greater significance after the Supreme Court in June struck down federal restrictions on spending coordinated between parties and their candidates, siding with Republican challengers including Vice President JD Vance. Since the June ruling, Republican committees have blown past the former limits ahead of the midterms. The two Republican committees have exceeded the ​former national caps by more than $48 million, according to Federal ‌Election Commission spending disclosures for July and August. Their Democratic counterparts also eclipsed the former limits, but by much less — just under $4 million. The three ​main national Republican committees ended August with about $233 million in cash. Their Democratic counterparts held roughly $130 million but also carried nearly $18 million in ​debt, according to Federal Election Commission filings. (Reporting by John Kruzel; Editing by Will Dunham) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/us-supreme-court-again-backs-204225313.html

item.title: U.S. considering using a non-nuclear 'mother of all bombs' against Iran, sources say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB) weapon at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, on March 11, 2003. - Department of Defense/Getty Images/File The US military has developed new strike plans that include potentially using the so-called “mother of all bombs” to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites should President Donald Trump give the order to resume combat operations either before or after the midterm elections, according to multiple US officials familiar with the matter. Using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb or MOAB, the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal, for the first time in the conflict with Iran would mark a notable escalation, even though there are doubts over how effective it would be in accomplishing any of Trump’s stated strategic objectives or tipping the balance of the war, multiple sources familiar with internal military planning discussions about potentially deploying the weapon said. Trump is facing pressure to bring an end to the deeply unpopular war — as Republicans brace for potential political backlash from voters in the upcoming midterm elections and there is little indication the two countries are close to a negotiated resolution after more than six months of US bombing. While the US military continues to provide Trump with options for potential strikes against outstanding Iranian targets, some officials continue to privately question whether the White House has a strategy that incorporates those plans in a way that could actually end the war — something only the president has the power to do. For months, Trump and his advisers have discussed options that could act as a “definitive” end to the war, at least from a messaging point of view, aware of how unpopular the conflict has become among Americans. While some administration figures have characterized the war as essentially won, Trump has been more guarded in recent remarks, stopping short of declaring victory and saying the US still has unfinished business in the country. Behind the scenes, Trump has also cast doubt on some outside allies who have encouraged him to simply bring US troops home and move on. Doing so, Trump has argued, would look like defeat. Over the course of the last several weeks, White House advisers have held meetings to discuss various options for Iran. While Trump announced publicly that he would not take new actions before the midterms, several advisers said privately they didn’t know whether that statement was definitive or could change before Election Day. Trump has ordered the military to develop additional strike packages against Iranian targets that include “a lot of energy infrastructure” and the potential use of a MOAB, one of the sources told CNN. The same source said the phrasing used was that this attack would come “prior to US retrograde in CENTCOM AOR (area of responsibility),” indicating the administration could launch the additional strikes, attempt to declare victory and quickly pull everyone out. A second source told CNN that military plans for striking Iranian nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain , also explicitly call for using the MOAB. In recent months, Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike Pickaxe, where the US and Israel believe Tehran has stored components of its nuclear program, even after pausing full combat operations earlier this year, and Trump continues to emphasize that his goal is to ensure Iran never obtains a nuclear weapon. Doubts MOAB would be effective Another US official noted that when the military plans, it develops a menu of options for policymakers that range from the high-end to low-end. Higher-end targets, including those that are located deep underground, require bigger bombs, and the MOAB is the biggest, the official added. But there are questions around whether the MOAB would be an effective munition to use against Iran’s nuclear facilities and other sites that are located deep underground. While the GPS-guided bomb is capable of destroying an area equivalent to nine city blocks, it likely lacks the capability to penetrate deep enough under the surface to destroy the suspected nuclear facilities at Pickaxe, which is believed to be fortified by layers of granite, and other remaining Iranian nuclear sites, sources said. The GBU-43/B, also known as the Massive Ordnance Air Blast, detonates during a test at Eglain Air Force Base, Florida, on November 21, 2003. - US Air Force/Handout/Reuters “The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” a third source familiar with military planning discussions around Iran told CNN. “It is definitely not designed as a deep penetration warhead.” If used, the MOAB would have devastating effects on the area that it impacts but likely only at the surface level, the sources noted. And the bomb’s massive blast radius would almost certainly raise concerns about the prospect of civilian casualties — particularly if it is used to target Iranian infrastructure targets located near populated areas and in close proximity to non-military sites. Still, Trump could opt to use the MOAB as a psychological weapon at a time when the Iranian regime appears dug in and unwilling to bend to his diplomatic demands. While US officials warn that deploying it is unlikely to force Iran’s capitulation or achieve a strategic military victory — it could provide Trump with an additional option, short of restarting full combat operations, to alter the conflict’s current status quo. “POTUS has unfortunately put himself in a situation where he is almost compelled to do something and, without the ammunition designed to penetrate that level … you have to look at psychological effects for which the MOAB is well-equipped,” the third source familiar with recent planning discussions added. Many within the administration as well as outside analysts agree that the only way to decisively defeat Iran would be through a major operation involving ground troops, a commitment that could potentially cost thousands of American lives. The Pentagon considers all scenarios, so those plans exist, but as of now no one in the administration is arguing for such drastic action. Trump has indicated he has little interest in putting US boots on the ground in Iran but his desire to end the conflict as soon as possible presents a political dilemma for a president who is keenly aware of how unpopular the war has become yet has been unable to secure a diplomatic agreement that would bring it to a close. Top Trump administration officials and military planners have been focused, for weeks, on finding an off-ramp that gives Trump a “symbolic” win — at minimum — he can try to sell to the American people without preventing a potential diplomatic breakthrough, starting with an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, CNN has reported. A fourth source familiar with the Pentagon’s recent planning discussions on Iran told CNN that military officials had developed some options that would amount to a “fireworks show,” with the goal of providing Trump an off-ramp from the conflict even if those strikes fail to accomplish his stated goals for starting the war in the first place. And despite Trump’s recent pledge to hold off on launching additional strikes before the midterms, the US military already appears to be preparing for potential Iranian retaliation should the president give the go-order. The next turnover of US troops deployed to CENTCOM is also expected to take place within the next few weeks, according to a fifth source, a US official who acknowledged it is possible some of the personnel who rotate out of the region, may not be replaced by fresh service members. Asked about the plans, a White House official told CNN that they do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist, adding “President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon.” In response to CNN’s request for comment, a Pentagon official said: “The Department of War plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary‑level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment.” MOAB developed for ‘psychological operations’ Developed during the Iraq War, the MOAB is an air blast-type warhead that explodes before hitting the ground to project a massive explosion from all sides. During the final stages of testing in 2003 , military officials told CNN the MOAB was mainly conceived as a weapon employed for “psychological operations.” Military officials said then they hoped such a huge blast would rattle Iraqi troops and pressure them into surrendering or not even fighting. As originally conceived, the MOAB was to be used against large formations of troops and equipment or hardened above-ground bunkers. The target set has been expanded to include targets buried under softer surfaces, such as caves or tunnels. Trump was the first US president to deploy the MOAB, during his first term when he authorized the military to use its most powerful non-nuclear bomb on ISIS positions in Afghanistan in 2017. unknown content item - That strike targeted a network of fortified underground tunnels that ISIS had been using to stage attacks on government forces — killing 36 ISIS fighters, Afghan officials said. The blast destroyed three underground tunnels as well as weapons and ammunition, but no civilians were hurt, Afghan and US officials added at the time. At the time, the bombing marked a dramatic change in attitude for Trump , who advocated an isolationist, “America first” foreign policy during his first election campaign. Following the 2017 strike, US military officials were pressed on whether the 21,600-pound bomb was necessary for that particular target and would likely face similar questions if the munition is deployed against Iran. item.title: Trump says he's 'very proud' as he unveils newly renovated White House facade
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump has shared new images of what he described as the “fully renovated” White House facade, saying extensive restoration work has given the historic building decades of additional life. Trump posted photographs of the South side of the White House to Truth Social early Thursday, highlighting restoration of the exterior as well as a new South Entrance and helipad. “Actual pictures of our fully renovated White House facade, facing South, with the new South Entrance, and Heliport!” Trump wrote. “It had to be done, and I am very proud to be the President who did it!” Trump added. President Donald Trump is seen on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, D.C., on September 26, 2026. The work comes amid a much broader transformation of the White House complex during Trump’s second term, including work on the North Portico, changes to the Rose Garden and extensive construction on the site of the former East Wing for a new ballroom and military complex. Trump said Thursday that the ballroom and military complex were “on time, and on budget,” describing them as an “unbelievably beautiful addition” to the White House. The project has been the subject of legal challenges and scrutiny over its cost and funding, with the Supreme Court allowing construction to continue in August while litigation over the project proceeds. Newsweek has contacted the White House and National Park Service for further comment. The South Lawn of the White House in Washington, DC, as seen March 20, 2009. What Changed at the White House? Trump’s newly released photographs focus on the South facade, one of the most recognizable views of the White House. The South Portico, with its curved colonnade and Truman Balcony above it, faces the South Lawn and has historically served as an arrival and departure point for presidents and foreign leaders. Trump said the work addressed deterioration to both the building’s exterior walls and decorative architectural features. “Over the years, the facade, both North and South, suffered tremendous wear, tear, and damage,” he wrote. “The exterior walls and ornamentation, both missing and in bad condition, has been fully restored to the Highest Level, giving the White House many decades of additional life!” The president did not provide a detailed breakdown of the restoration work or its cost. Work has also been underway on the White House’s North Portico. The Washington Post reported in September that workers had spent roughly two months repairing the historic columns and strengthening the entrance before coverings surrounding the structure began to be removed. The White House itself dates to the 1790s, although the building has repeatedly been rebuilt, expanded and renovated. The South Portico was constructed during James Monroe’s presidency in the 1820s, while the North Portico was added several years later under Andrew Jackson. The West Wing was constructed during Theodore Roosevelt’s presidency in 1902 and the White House underwent a near-total interior reconstruction during Harry Truman’s presidency between 1948 and 1952. An image posted on Truth Social shows the newly renovated White House facade. Trump’s White House Renovations The facade restoration is part of a series of changes Trump has made to the White House and its grounds, among the most significant being the ballroom and associated East Wing redevelopment. The original East Wing was demolished as the administration moved ahead with plans for a large new ceremonial space and additional security and military infrastructure. Trump initially promoted the ballroom as a privately funded addition designed to give the White House a permanent space for large state events rather than relying on temporary tents. The project has since expanded to include substantial underground security infrastructure and other facilities. In August, the Supreme Court permitted construction to continue while a lawsuit brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation proceeds. The Court said its ruling did not decide the ultimate legality of the project but found that the government was likely to prevail on its argument that the preservation group lacked standing. Trump has repeatedly said taxpayers will not pay for the ballroom itself. In September, he said the ballroom would cost close to $400 million and was being funded by himself and private companies. Internal contractor documents reported by The Washington Post , however, estimated the wider East Wing project at about $600 million, with approximately $293 million expected from private sources and the remainder associated with government-funded security, military and Executive Residence work. The White House has said those taxpayer-funded costs relate to security and other government functions rather than the ballroom itself. Trump reiterated Thursday that the work remained on schedule. “Likewise, the Ballroom and Military Complex, is on time, and on budget,” he wrote. Trump said the development would be the most significant addition to the White House since the West Wing was constructed. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Tobias Meyjes and Tony Phillips . item.title: Car payments just hit a record $787 a month—and 1 in 4 new-car buyers is now signing a 7-year loan
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
American drivers face a daunting market. The average monthly payment on a financed new car hit a record $787 in the third quarter, according to Edmunds , up from $777 in the second quarter and $756 a year earlier. Buyers are also borrowing more than ever. The average amount financed climbed to a record $44,664, while the average new vehicle sold for $50,562 in September, per Kelley Blue Book , just $52 shy of the all-time high. Nationwide, auto loan balances reached $1.71 trillion in the second quarter, according to the New York Fed , roughly 56% more than a decade earlier . For Joseph Yoon, consumer insights analyst at Edmunds, the math is brutally simple: Vehicle prices sit near record highs, and interest rates remain stubbornly elevated, with the average new-car APR holding at 7%. “Mix those things together and then you get record-high monthly payments,” Yoon told Fortune . “Just how the math works out.” The road that led to record car payments So how exactly did we arrive here? Yoon points to the pandemic as a significant precursor to the state of car sales. When factories shut down and parts ran short, manufacturers faced a choice: build fewer cars, or build the ones with higher margins. They chose the latter. “Automakers realize, ‘Hey, even if we lose a couple million units across the board, if we have high margins, our profits look great,’” Yoon said. “And that’s perfectly fine. But as consumers, we drew the short straw, and have to pay for elevated prices.” The result: New vehicles now cost about 30% more than they did six years ago, as Fortune has reported . For buyers struggling to afford today’s prices, the dealership finance office offers a tempting solution: stretch the loan. Indeed, a record share of new-car buyers decided that a seven-year loan sounded less scary than the alternative. In the third quarter, 25.5% of financed new-car purchases carried terms of 84 months or more, according to Edmunds , up from 23.9% the prior quarter and 21.8% a year earlier. Even so, a record 21.2% of buyers committed to monthly payments of $1,000 or more. But longer terms carry consequences, some of which aren’t immediately obvious. “The longer you have a loan term, technically the longer you’re paying just toward interest, not toward the principal of the loan, especially when the interest rates are so high,” Yoon said. The average amount of interest paid over the life of a new-car loan reached a record $9,938 in the third quarter, up from $9,442 a year earlier, Edmunds found. That increase came even though rates didn’t budge; Edmunds attributed it to buyers financing larger amounts over longer periods. Helen Colby, an assistant teaching professor at Carnegie Mellon University’s Tepper School of Business, told Fortune that the true cost of an 84-month loan can go well beyond the accumulation of interest. “For borrowers who already have tight budgets, getting such a long loan means committing themselves to five, six, or even seven years of increased spending that will reduce their budget for other things like vacations, savings, or even necessities like food and clothing,” Colby said. And there are no signs of imminent relief. The average APR on new-car loans was 7% in the third quarter, unchanged from the previous quarter and a year earlier. “Especially towards the end of the year, I don’t think anything’s going to change,” Yoon said. Are car buyers reaching a breaking point? Logic would suggest that at a certain point, buyers would simply refuse to pay such prices for cars. If there is a tipping point, though, it’s still on the horizon, Yoon said. “We keep thinking that there might be some type of tipping point. Are sales going to crater? And we haven’t seen anything like that. Sales are fine,” Yoon said. “Despite these record prices, despite the kind of overall ‘bad vibes’ in the economy for most people, car sales haven’t really suffered all that much, if at all.” Edmunds’ head of insights, Jessica Caldwell, called the latest data “a remarkable display of consumer resilience” in the company’s quarterly report. The reason points to a phenomenon economists call the “K-shaped economy.” “The people that are buying new cars tend to be households with six-figure incomes,” Yoon said. The share of new-car buyers earning less than $100,000 fell to 37% last year from 50% in 2020, according to Cox Automotive . So although many people feel priced out of a new car, there’s no shortage of buyers at the top to make up the difference. Buyers at the bottom of the K-shaped economy feel the pinch Fortune spoke with one person feeling the crunch of the new-car market. Abbey Burbach, 35, said she can’t afford a new car despite working three jobs totaling 50 to 60 hours a week. “You’re lucky to find a new car for under $400 a month anymore.” Burbach said most of her peers who drive newer-model cars didn’t buy them; they inherited them from benevolent elders. “I know a lot of people who basically begged their parents not to trade in their car,” she said. The trend is more than anecdotal, Yoon said: The average age of a new-car buyer has been rising. “It was on a downward trend for a while, but it’s gone up the last couple of years because, again, young people in this kind of market are finding it more and more difficult to be able to buy a car.” The used car market offers little relief For buyers priced out of new cars, the used market has always been the fallback plan. That calculus isn’t so simple anymore. When new-car inventory dried up during the pandemic, buyers flooded the used market instead, and prices responded quickly, Yoon said. The average used-vehicle transaction price rose from $20,942 in the second quarter of 2020 to $27,306 by the third quarter of 2021, according to Edmunds data . Today, used-car buyers who finance borrow an average of $30,703 at a 10.6% APR, Edmunds says . Those prices have largely stayed put, thanks in part to a slump in leasing. Before the pandemic, leases made up roughly 30% of new-vehicle deals, according to J.D. Power. That share fell to 17% during the shortage and had recovered only to about 23% in the first half of 2026, the firm’s data shows . Why does it matter? Because leased cars are a primary source of used inventory for dealers once they’re returned. “These cars come back within 24 to 48 months, or typically 36 months,” Yoon said. “And when that source dries up, literally millions of used cars that are supposed to come back to dealer lots every year aren’t coming back anymore. That has had a pretty dramatic impact on pricing used cars.” Some help is on the way: Off-lease volume is expected to climb to about 2.66 million vehicles this year and 3.29 million in 2027, up from roughly 2.15 million in 2025, according to Experian estimates cited by JPMorgan . For now, though, buyers are still feeling the squeeze from every direction. “We have this huge revolving circle of negative effects on the market for the consumer,” Yoon said. “There’s nowhere you can catch a break.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com This article originally appeared on Fortune at https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/car-payments-just-hit-record-141354915.html

item.title: Beef prices are soaring — and now meat is a midterm election issue
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
In the midterm elections , meat is on the menu. As Democrats and Republicans argue over high prices and the Iran war , they're also having a food fight over who's the most red-blooded carnivore. The latest example came this week in Mississippi, where Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom released a video with a snippet of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith saying that if consumers are upset over high beef prices, “you know you have so many proteins to choose from.” The video cuts to a man grilling burgers who says, “Pick another protein? I'd rather pick another senator instead.” The Mississippi race is somewhat unusual because it's the Democrat hammering the Republican over beef. Elsewhere, Republicans have branded Democrats as vegans or otherwise opposed to meat, trying to show that they're culturally out of step with voters, hostile to local cattle industries or just not manly enough. In Texas, Republicans seized on an old interview in which Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico boasted that his campaign, then for the Texas statehouse, was going vegan. Talarico has since been publicly scarfing down barbecue to rebut allegations that his dietary choices mean he's not a real Texan. In Colorado, Republicans have gone after Democratic congressional candidate Manny Rutinel for his activism against meat production and factory farming. In college, he was photographed shirtless with a banner for the People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals around his chest. In 2021, Rutinel founded Climate Refarm, which advocated for cutting down on the use of meat and has signed onto letters advocating for raising taxes on meat and dairy. He also supported a 2024 ballot measure to ban a lamb slaughterhouse in Denver, which failed. Rutinel, 31, is now running against Republican Rep. Gabe Evans in Colorado's 8th district, which includes a vast swath of the northeastern part of the state dotted with ranches, dairy farms and meat processing facilities, including the headquarters of beef production titan JBS Swift. Republicans have hammered Rutinel over advocating veganism, to the point that the conservative media group Daily Wire this week released an undercover video of a campaign official saying Rutinel eats meat “as little as possible.” Rutinel, who's made a point of publicly eating steak tacos on the campaign trail, scoffed at such arguments in an interview after a recent campaign stop. “I don't think Coloradans care about what's on my plate," he said. “I think they care more about what's on theirs.” Evans said the issue goes beyond Rutinel's meal preferences. “I don't care what he eats personally,” Evans said in an interview. “I care that he wants to use the power of the government to make everyone eat that way.” Republicans have gone after two other Democratic House candidates on meat — hammering Lindsay James in Iowa's 2nd district, an area filled with hog farms, for supporting “meatless May” in a 2020 Facebook post, and Amish Shah in Arizona's 1st district for his longstanding vegetarianism and animal rights activism. Also in Iowa, Republican Senate candidate and current Rep. Ashley Hinson slammed her opponent, state lawmaker Josh Turek, for opposing a bill banning lab-grown meat from being sold in the state. “He’d rather have meat that comes from a lab than from our family farms,” she said at a campaign appearance. Democrats have hammered on meat as well, but mainly just as one of the staples that cost more under Trump, squeezing voters' pocketbooks. Trump has tried to lower prices by opening U.S. markets to beef imports, especially from Argentina, which is governed by a close Trump ally. However, those moves have angered U.S. producers as prices have remained stubbornly high, creating a potential weakness in Republican-leaning states where Democrats hope to gain ground this year. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the average pound of ground beef cost $6.79 last month, up from $5.55 in January of 2025, when Trump returned to office. That was the dynamic that Hyde-Smith, a cattle rancher and former state agriculture commissioner, was addressing in her interview that was clipped in Colom's video. The prosecutor — who also delivers the “pick another senator” line in the spot — is running a longshot challenge in Mississippi. A spokesman for Hyde-Smith's campaign argued that the Democrats deserve blame for high prices. “It is Scott Colom who supports Biden-era policies that drove up inflation,” said Nathan Calvert. ___ Associated Press writer Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, contributed to this report.
