item.title: Reflecting Pool liner failed in 85 places, inspection finds
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A recently applied blue coating on the bottom of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was damaged in at least 85 places after workers rushed to refill the pool before the Donald Trump-requested liner had set. A report commissioned by the contractor that did the work, obtained by The Washington Post , does not make any mention of vandalism despite the president’s ongoing claims and sworn statements from administration officials that attributed the peeled-off lining to “botched installation.” The report instead blames a rushed job to meet Trump’s demands that the work be completed for the nation’s 250th anniversary on July 4. The 75-page “failure analysis” by Atlantic Coating Inspection reveals that Trump’s “American flag blue” coating buckled along eight of the 10 expansion joints on the pool’s basin. The liner also blistered in nearly 40 places due to moisture or chemical fumes trapped beneath it, and the paint peeled in nearly two dozen spots before detaching from the pool floor and flapping to the surface, the report found. A ‘failure analysis’ found more than 85 damage points at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool that compromised a recently applied blue liner after Donald Trump pushed for renovations this summer (Reuters) The Trump administration has funneled nearly $20 million in taxpayer funding into the project despite the president’s initial estimate that the renovation could be done quickly for just $1.5 million. That was in April. The liner was finally replaced in recent weeks and the pool is being refilled, again, this week. Initial costs quickly surged to nearly $7 million this summer after an initial no-bid contract was handed to a Virginia-based firm that did not appear to have previously held a contract with the federal government. That company, Atlantic Industrial Coatings LLC, was awarded another $6.2 million in May, according to federal spending records. On June 3, the company received another $1 million — followed by more than $461,000 on June 15. The shallow pool, which the president repeatedly promotes as “bigger than skyscrapers,” was initially refurbished this summer with a shade of dark blue and outfitted with “advanced nanobubbler technology” to tackle algae blooms that have long plagued the landmark. But shortly after workers refilled the pool, the algae returned, and the recently applied sealant in the Trump-requested blue hue started to peel and float to the surface. The monument was then closed off with fencing and the pool was drained once again to repair the damage and redo the work. In July, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said the Trump administration would not seek any new contracts after costs for the project exploded to more than $17 million. But spending records show that the National Park Service awarded a nearly $2.7 million contract to American Ag Energy Inc. the following month for the maintenance, repair and rebuilding of water purification and sewage treatment equipment. Another firm, Ohio-based Green Water Solutions, also known as Greenwater Services, was also awarded $1.8 million to install a water-purification system. Workers have been forced to drain the pool and re-do renovations after administration officials admitted that damage to the monument was due to ‘botched’ construction, not vandalism, despite the president’s claims (AP) The Department of Interior skipped a typical competitive bidding process to hand out millions of taxpayer dollars to a handful of companies for the work, claiming that “only a limited pool of contractors possess the qualification and equipment” for the work, Officials claimed that the need for renovations was so urgent that any delays would cause “serious injury” to the government, though it remains unclear what that “injury” entailed. In July, weeks after U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro publicly accused a former Olympian of “forcefully and violently” ripping out the blue liner, she dismissed a criminal case against him entirely. Pirro’s office admitted that the Trump-requested “American flag blue” sealant started to peel “almost immediately” after the work was completed after recent renovations to the site. The Department of Interior “provided less than fulsome information at the outset of this case,” the filing said. It was not until after the indictment was filed against 67-year-old David Hearn that the agency determined that the “damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism,” according to Pirro’s office. Trump later pushed Pirro to “revisit her hastily made decision,” though he has also admitted that “some contractor error” played a role in the damage. A judge in Washington, DC, has blocked prosecutors from trying to charge David Hearn a second time after the government dismissed a criminal case against him over damage to the monument (Getty) A judge later blocked prosecutors from trying to charge Hearn a second time , finding that a case against him would likely be the result of “political pressure” from the president. Earlier this month, D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman called that idea of prosecuting Hearn again “simply fanciful” and permanently tossed the case against him. Hearn’s attorneys have asked the Department of Justice and Department of Interior to launch an independent investigation into alleged “widespread misconduct” surrounding the case. The administration “subjected an innocent man to a nightmare of wrongful arrest, felony indictment, and public defamation to cover up their own botched, rushed renovation of the Reflecting Pool,” attorneys Michael Bromwich, Steve Levin, Norm Eisen and Mary Dohrmann said in a statement last week, “This administration threw the entire weight of the federal government into prosecuting Davey Hearn, and their actions surrounding his arrest and indictment demand full accountability,” they added. WASHINGTON (AP) — Wholesale inflation rose more than expected last month on a big jump in fuel costs , a sign that stubbornly rising prices remain an economic challenge for consumers and a political problem for Republicans in the midterm elections. Wholesale inflation rose more than expected last month on a big jump in fuel costs as rising prices become a bigger economic challenge for millions of Americans, and a growing political problem for Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections. The Labor Department’s producer price index — which captures inflation before it reaches consumers — soared 6.3% in September from a year ago, up from 5.6% in August and the biggest increase since December 2022, the government said Thursday. On a monthly basis, wholesale prices rose 1.3% from August to September, marking the largest increase since March 2022, after a 0.5% gain the previous month. Thursday’s data amplify the better-known consumer price index, released Wednesday, which also accelerated in September as gas prices jumped. A broad range of goods and services also got more expensive. Both inflation reports raise pressure on the inflation-fighters at the Federal Reserve to hike their key interest rate. Inflation has now topped the central bank’s 2% target for five and a half years. Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 0.7% from August to September, up sharply from 0.2% in the previous month. Compared with a year ago, core prices rose 5%, up from 4.6% in August. More expensive energy drove most of the increase as wholesale gas prices soared more than 20% from August to September. But the report also showed other costs rising, including those for electricity, vegetables, shipping, and air fares. Ongoing inflation has eroded Americans' incomes and soured most consumers on the economy. The Labor Department said Wednesday that average weekly paychecks, when adjusted for inflation, shrank last month compared with a year ago for the first time since May. Higher prices have also taken a toll on Trump’s standing with U.S. voters. A poll released this month by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of U.S. adults approve of Trump's handling of the cost of living. And only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low. The Federal Reserve, meanwhile, will hold a policy meeting in two weeks and are expected to keep its key short-term interest rate unchanged. item.title: Ukraine relies on Starlink to fight Russia. Now a sudden change threatens its drones.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Starlink terminals, which connect to thousands of SpaceX satellites in obit, are often camouflaged on the battlefield [Getty Images] Starlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on. For Ukraine, it is vital for communications on the battlefield and effective drone warfare. Using Starlink, Ukrainian drones can stay connected to operators over longer distances than conventional radio networks and are less vulnerable to jamming. But on Tuesday night, Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection . This disrupted some battlefield "missions", a top Ukrainian official said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks. The restriction at 100mph (160km/h) meant that any drone travelling faster than that lost connection and was effectively useless. "Starlink gives Ukraine the ability to see what's coming, to protect people," Kurt Volker, former US ambassador to Nato, told the BBC's Radio 4 Today programme. "If you cut that off, then more people are going to get killed - and that is a very cynical and callous decision to slow that down the way that has been done." Connectivity had been restored by Wednesday evening. The move has once again shown how Starlink can impact the conflict, which has been raging since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Operators use the Starlink network to stay connected to weapons like drones, so they can see targets in real time [Getty Images] What are Starlink and Starshield? Starlink is an internet network that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and battlefields. It currently relies on more than 10,000 active satellites, making Starlink the world's largest satellite constellation. It is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, and is the company's biggest revenue driver. While Starlink is for civilian use, Starshield is its military-grade sister service, designed for the Pentagon. Starshield relies on the Starlink network, but has greater security like enhanced encryption so that sensitive information can be transmitted without interception. The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February , giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict. How does Starlink work on a battlefield? Put simply, Starlink uses its thousands of satellites to ping high-speed internet back to almost every corner of the globe, using terminals on the ground that users can easily buy and set up themselves. As Musk said, they have two instructions: "point at sky, plug in". This makes them ideal for use on the battlefield. "It's a connection… that you can basically use pretty fast, you don't need any special equipment, you don't need to prepare, you just go to the field and usually it works," Neo, a soldier with one of Ukraine's drone reconnaissance units, told the Today programme. "It simplifies our work because we can translate or stream our reconnaissance operations," he added. The network has become "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", George Barros from the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces. [BBC] In Ukraine, both Starlink (the civilian service) and Starshield (the military service) are used, depending on what communications are needed. It is crucial for the effective use of weapons such as drones, which connect to the network so that operators can see their targets in real time, effectively minimising the time between "sensor-to shooter", Barros told the BBC. Because Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, when Ukraine sends long-range missiles deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work. When it comes to Ukraine's self-defence, it relies on the Starlink network to protect its own skies against incoming Russian attacks, especially jet-powered Shahed drones, Barros added. Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph (319 km/h), meaning the Starlink restriction made Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible. For Neo, this means that any deliberate restrictions on the Starlink network are "a betrayal". With no ready replacement for the Starlink network, any speed restrictions or loss of connectivity have major implications for Ukraine defences, and the recent limits have shown how dependent Kyiv is on the network. Starlink terminals, like this one in Ukraine's Donetsk region, are quick and easy to set up, making them ideal for use on the battlefield [Lev Radin/ Getty Images] While Starlink can provide access nearly everywhere in the world, that does not mean it can be accessed everywhere, and countries must be licenced to use it. Russia is one place where it is not authorised, although Kyiv has in the past said that Moscow was still getting hold of the terminals and using them in occupied territory in Ukraine. "If SpaceX obtains knowledge that Starlink terminal is being used by a sanctioned or unauthorized party, we investigate the claim and take actions to deactivate the terminal if confirmed," Starlink said in 2024. But with tens of thousands of terminals in Ukraine alone, it could be a near impossible task to determine which terminals are authorised and which ones are not. Why did Starlink restrict drone speeds? The answer remains unclear. During a visit to London on Wednesday, Zelensky had said he hoped it was just a mistake, however, in a later interview with the Financial Times, he said: "It was not a technical problem, it was the will." Musk said that Starshield is managed by the US government and suggested the Pentagon could be responsible. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote on X . "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS [the president of the United States]." He added: "Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company." The BBC has contacted the White House and Pentagon for comment. A Ukrainian soldier attaches a Starlink transmitter to a 'Vampire' attack drone in the Donetsk region, eastern Ukraine, in June [EPA] The restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that left 600,000 without power and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military. Residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit. "It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning. Relations between the US and Ukraine have worsened recently, especially since the US announced a deal with Russia to import its diesel into the American market. Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and in response Donald Trump said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president". On Sunday, Trump announced a ceasefire on energy infrastructure, but three days later, Ukraine said it would resume the strikes , accusing Russia of ignoring it (the Kremlin said it had never agreed to a ceasefire), and the US of withdrawing crucial support. Zelensky has accused the US of threatening to withhold intelligence if Ukraine continues striking Russian oil facilities. Trump has denied this, but last week told reporters that Zelensky had "better damn well stop" the strikes. While in London, Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US. Trump's deal with Russia is his administration's latest effort to lower US fuel prices ahead of next month's midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war. That conflict, which started in February, has seen prices skyrocket, souring his standing with the American public. item.title: Lawyers for New York man shot by ICE say officer fired into car without warning
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
NEW YORK (AP) — Lawyers for a man wounded by an immigration officer while driving with his young son in New York said in a court filing Wednesday that the agent who shot him never identified himself before he ran up to the car, smashed one of its windows, then fired several shots into the vehicle. The account by lawyers for Oscar Belgal contrasted sharply with the version of events outlined by Department of Homeland Security officials. They have said officers opened fire only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and “accelerated toward other officers.” The Legal Aid Society, in a petition filed in Brooklyn federal court seeking Belgal's release, said he had picked up his son from school on Oct. 8 and was stopped in front of a fire hydrant, looking for a parking spot, when “an anonymous, masked man” stormed up to the vehicle with his gun drawn, followed by other masked men with guns. “The men did not identify themselves, show any documents or otherwise communicate with Oscar in any substantive way," Belgal's lawyers wrote. "Instead, without identifying himself, the first man struck and shattered Oscar’s window and began firing a pistol into Oscar’s car while his son cowered in the back seat. One of those bullets struck Oscar in the neck and he immediately began to bleed.” New York City police security camera footage released by the department last week shows some of the encounter but doesn't conclusively resolve the dispute about how the shooting happened. The video shows a man wearing a sweatshirt and a red hat running up to the car with his gun pointed at Belgal, then immediately using the barrel of his gun to bash the driver’s side window. The window shatters on the second blow. A second officer comes into view alongside the car and draws his gun. Belgal then pulls into the street, away from the two officers. The car pulls out of view of the camera, with the officer in the red hat in pursuit. Whatever happened next didn't appear on the NYPD's security cameras, but the chase ended just a moment later, with Belgal's damaged car resting against a concrete barrier with bullet holes in its windshield and a rear window. Video from bystanders and NYPD body camera footage show that ICE officers handcuffed Belgal and tended to a gunshot wound to his neck as he sat on the pavement outside the car. NYPD officers took Belgal to a nearby hospital. DHS didn't comment Wednesday on the claims by Belgal's lawyers, saying the incident remains under investigation. But DHS officials have maintained that ICE officers fired their weapons because they believed their lives were in danger . Belgal’s lawyers said he didn’t learn the men were ICE officers until he awoke later in the hospital. They say he remains detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, where he has yet to receive surgery to remove the bullet lodged in his neck. They also say he has lost sensation on the left side of his face and is suffering from impaired hearing. “Mr. Belgal’s detention was unlawful from its inception. ICE officers shot him in the neck in front of his five year-old son, failed to provide him with immediate medical assistance, and now continue to hold him in a facility notorious for medical neglect,” said Perry McAninch and Elyssa Williams, the lawyers representing Belgal. DHS referred questions about Belgal's medical treatment to the Federal Bureau of Prisons, which manages the jail. That agency also declined comment, citing “privacy, safety, and security reasons,” but said, in general, that it “does not deny any inmate necessary medical treatment or basic necessities.” At a news conference last week, Marcos Charles, the head of ICE's enforcement and removal operations, said Belgal refused orders to exit his vehicle and then accelerated and smashed into two government vehicles as ICE officers tried to block him from driving away. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has maintained officers didn’t know a child was in the car and blamed Belgal for putting his son's life in danger. ___ Associated Press reporter Valerie Gonzalez in McAllen, Texas, contributed to this story. Police are investigating a report that a woman was sexually assaulted during a fraternity party near the University of Chicago campus, an allegation that has drawn widespread attention as colleges and fraternities face renewed scrutiny over sexual violence and campus safety . The incident was reported shortly after 2 a.m. local time on Oct. 11 at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity house, according to the University of Chicago Police Department's daily crime log . The log states that "a victim reported being sexually assaulted by an unknown suspect while at a party" at the off-campus residence. The University of Chicago, a private school with about 18,000 students enrolled, said in a statement that a woman who is not affiliated with the school reported that she was sexually assaulted at around 1:50 a.m. local time during a party at the fraternity house. Another person intervened, and the suspect fled before police arrived. In an update on Oct. 13, the university said a person of interest had been identified through witness statements and video evidence from university cameras and license-plate readers. The person of interest is not a student, has no affiliation with the school, and has been banned from campus. University officials said the school's Department of Safety and Security shared the evidence with the Chicago Police Department, which is leading the criminal investigation. As of Oct. 14, the Chicago Police Department said no arrest had been made and that the investigation remained ongoing. "Since the CPD investigation is still active and charges have not been filed, the University is not at liberty to disclose the name of the person of interest," the university said in the statement. "Separate from CPD’s ongoing investigation, the University will continue to determine whether violations of University policy occurred, and will initiate disciplinary actions as warranted." USA TODAY reached out to the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity for comment. 'I was brutalized': Cornell rape allegations, investigation, lawsuit Report: Group allegedly cheered as woman was sexually assaulted The Chicago Police Department confirmed to USA TODAY on Oct. 14 that a 21-year-old woman reported the assault to police and "self-transported" to University of Chicago Hospital for treatment. According to The Chicago Sun-Times , which obtained a police report, the victim told police she had been dancing and drinking at the fraternity party before she "began feeling unwell." She reported being sexually assaulted inside the fraternity house. The newspaper reported that two friends of the woman told police they forced their way into a bathroom to intervene and a group of men attempted to block them from entering. The men were seen "cheering and appearing to encourage the activity inside," according to the report cited by the Sun-Times. The woman's friends found her and a man inside the bathroom, both partially undressed, the newspaper reported. The woman was described in the report as "not fully conscious," according to the Sun-Times. The Sun-Times reported that one friend told the man to get off the woman, and "he responded that everything was 'cool.'" The newspaper also reported that when the woman and her friends later confronted the man outside the fraternity house, another man claimed they had identified the wrong person and directed them elsewhere before fleeing. One of the victim's friends briefly pursued the man before encountering a university police officer and reporting the incident, according to the Sun-Times. 'Baffling': Early Cornell rape investigation troubles experts Fraternities under renewed scrutiny nationwide The University of Chicago described the report as "deeply concerning" and said supporting the alleged victim and assisting police remain priorities. University officials noted that fraternities are not recognized student organizations at the university and are not formally affiliated with the school, though students remain subject to university policies and disciplinary procedures. The reported assault comes at a time of heightened national attention on sexual violence allegations connected to college campuses . Much of that attention has centered on Cornell University , where a woman alleged in a lawsuit that she was drugged and repeatedly sexually assaulted by fraternity members during an incident in 2024. The allegations became public last month and sparked criticism of the school's handling of the case. Though Cornell conducted its own investigation and imposed disciplinary actions, no criminal charges were filed. The men accused in the lawsuit have denied wrongdoing. In response to the controversy, Cornell University announced this week that it is suspending fraternity events through the rest of this academic year, saying it plans to involve the New York State Police in future investigations of campus sexual assault allegations. The changes came amid mounting pressure from students and advocacy groups seeking a stronger response to reports of sexual misconduct. Fraternities have also come under increased scrutiny at the University of Arizona , which earlier this month temporarily suspended fraternity activities following reports of assault, hazing, and other misconduct . "If that reporting is accurate, Ms. Zacharia has repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practice law without a license to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime," the complaint stated. Rick Coca, a spokesperson for the State Bar of California, confirmed the agency had no record of Zacharia being licensed in California under her married or maiden names. "Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie," CfA Executive Director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a news release. "In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime," she said. White House Communications Director Steven Cheung responded on X , calling CfA a "radical-leftist organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome." "Nobody takes them seriously because they are deranged low lifes," Cheung wrote. InfluenceWatch, a project of the conservative Capital Research Center, describes CfA as a left-of-center advocacy group that frequently targets Republican officials and conservative organizations. It notes the group was founded by former staff members of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Government and has two prominent Democrat political operatives on its board. The complaint cites several instances in which Zacharia described herself as a lawyer, including an Oct. 5 appearance on Newsmax anchor Greg Kelly’s WABC radio show, when she invoked her legal background while discussing the Senate’s use of blue slips in the confirmation process for U.S. attorneys. It also questions her reported tenure as general counsel for Fix California, a nonprofit founded by former Trump administration official Richard Grenell, from January 2024 to March 2025. CfA acknowledged it is unknown whether Zacharia performed legal work for Fix California and asked the State Bar to investigate her responsibilities. Under California law, unauthorized practice of law or unlawfully representing oneself as entitled to practice law can constitute a misdemeanor punishable by up to a year in county jail, a $1,000 fine, or both. The complaint asks regulators to consider referring the matter to prosecutors if violations are established. Zacharia, who graduated from Pepperdine University School of Law in 2011, previously worked for the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing. Asked Wednesday where she passed the bar exam, Zacharia responded , "when I moved to China." item.title: As inflation rises, poll finds 4 in 10 Americans struggle to afford basic necessities
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
More than 4 in 10 Americans said they are struggling to afford basic living costs amid rising inflation levels in the country, according to polling data released Wednesday. The Pew Research Center surveys , which were conducted in late July and August, found that 44 percent of U.S. adults reported struggling to pay for basic necessities like medical care, rent or mortgage, transportation and food. Rising costs had an even greater impact on lower income Americans, as 71 percent of those surveyed said they struggled with costs for at least one of these expense categories. Additionally, 60 percent of people said they did not have enough income to “lead the kind of life they want,” while 53 percent said they did not have sufficient emergency funds. The inflation rate in August was 3.4 percent , down from 3.7 percent in July. Since then, the Bureau of Labor Statistics has reported further increases to the consumer price index, including a 0.6 percent increase in September. Gas prices have accounted for a sizable share of the inflation rate increases, as the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war placed a sustained strain on global energy supplies. A gallon of regular gas was around $4.33 a gallon in the U.S. on Wednesday afternoon, up from about $3.08 a year ago, according to AAA . The average cost of diesel has also spiked to more than $6 a gallon — an increase of more than $2 from last year. President Trump has attempted to calm concerns about rising costs of living amid this conflict and his administration’s tariff fight with Canada ahead of the midterm elections, in which affordability is expected to be a top issue for voters at the ballot box. During a Tuesday campaign rally in Alaska, the president did not offer hope that the months-long conflict was nearing a close, telling the crowd he has “had it” with Iran’s leaders and added that his administration was “going to do a number” on the country. The Pew report released Wednesday was based on findings from two surveys among a sample of 5,166 U.S. adults with a margin of error of approximately 1.6 percentage points. item.title: Major U.S. banks turned away customers over political and religious views, report says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Comptroller of the Currency says the nation's nine largest banks denied financial services to customers based on their political, religious, or social beliefs, according to a regulatory review released Wednesday. The OCC reviewed nearly 100,000 complaints and received approximately 50,000 documents from JPMorgan Chase Bank, Bank of America, Citibank, Wells Fargo Bank, U.S. Bank, Capital One, PNC Bank, TD Bank, and BMO Bank regarding their policies, procedures, practices, and individual customer decisions. The federal banking watchdog determined that the banks' sweeping internal guidelines lacked objective, risk-based criteria, effectively shutting out legitimate customers and businesses based on ideological leanings rather than financial risk. The OCC said its findings reveal a systematic effort within the banking sector to restrict access for politically sensitive industries through both public and nonpublic policies. Federal regulators found that lenders restricted certain sectors' access to financial services, including oil and gas exploration; coal mining; firearms or ammunition manufacturing or distribution; construction or operation of detention facilities; and the manufacturing, distribution or online retail of tobacco or e-cigarettes. The Trump administration has voiced growing concerns over "de-banking" and the use of the financial system to achieve social and political objectives. "Today's report provides irrefutable evidence that the nation's largest banks have denied, debanked, and discriminated against customers and lawful businesses," said Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould. "Americans should have access to financial services regardless of their beliefs, affiliations, or political views. " All nine banks report having reassessed the role of reputation risk in decisions to accept or terminate new customers, according to the OCC's report. Several banks said they had minimized reliance on reputation risk, and bank employees now must consider it in the context of other financial or business consequences, including credit risk, money laundering and terrorist financing risk. The Bank Policy Institute, a lobbying group that represents the banks, said in a statement in reaction to the report, "We support efforts to establish clear and consistent standards that promote access while maintaining sound risk management, including the administration's recent efforts to prioritize supervisory attention on material financial risk and rather than reputational risk." The group also noted it would continue to work with the administration and Congress on proposals that ensure that political or religious beliefs do not unfairly affect customers' access to banking services. JPMorgan Chase said in a statement, "We take this seriously, learned from it, and improved the way we do business. We agree with the Administration on a broader point: years of operating in a regulatory environment that often second-guessed decisions contributed to a culture of caution across the banking industry. That system needs fixing." The bank says its policies prohibit discrimination against customers based on political or religious views. A spokesperson for Wells Fargo and Citigroup declined to comment on the OCC's report, while PNC said it was reviewing the findings. Bank of America, U.S. Bank and Capital One had not responded for comment as of this writing. The review was directed by President Trump's executive order, "Guaranteeing Fair Access to Banking for All Americans," to determine whether these banks' policies or practices required or influenced banks to deny or limit access to financial services to Americans because of their political or religious beliefs or lawful business activities. The OCC is considering further actions and writing new rules to prevent banks from discriminating against customers or prospective customers based on their political or religious beliefs. The OCC is also coordinating its debanking review with the reviews of other federal and state partners. "Notwithstanding certain efforts by the largest banks to rein in these practices, I am not confident that they will be enough," said Gould.
